newsitem.title: UK: Coffee could yet look dizzy, data is awaited.
newsitem.headline: Coffee could yet look dizzy, data is awaited.

text.p: Coffee prices have soared 35-40 percent in world markets this year in a stunning rally, but it could now be open to an ambush by speculators tempted to lock in their gains.
Analysts say the news so far in 1997 has all been bullish, from talk of a lower-than-expected crop in Brazil to labour unrest in number two producer Colombia, against a backdrop of low stocks.
But any data suggesting that the supply prospect is not as tight as it seems or more chart signals that the market is overbought might trigger a sell-off, say some London dealers.

Prices hit $1,680 per tonne for the London Robustas on Tuesday and the rally has led to retail price rises in Europe and the United States, on a view that stocks are too low to allow any disruption to supply.
But while some analysts reckon the Robustas are set to conquer $1,800, others, at least in London, are less enthusiastic and suggest that speculative funds may yet spoil the party.

"At some stage the bubble will burst. The funds will have to liquidate their positions," said one London trader, adding that some had jumped into coffee for the first time and may sell at the first sign of a downturn.
The rally has exceeded most analysts' targets and London's May Robusta contract seemed to be nervous above $1,600.
It hit $1,680 on Tuesday after it chased New York Arabicas which rose to hit 20-month highs at $167.50/lb basis March on Wednesday.
Technical indicators are signalling overbought and the $1,600 level which some analysts see as key to maintain the upside momentum seems to be too exposed after Wednesday profit taking.
Moreover, the fundamental tightness that keeps fuelling Arabica just doesn't exist in Robusta where supplies are more than adequate for consumption.
Yet, many analysts remain bullish for both markets in the long-term, despite increases in retail prices in some European countries and in the United States that may stifle consumer demand.
"Retail levels are very low and the price increases are relatively modest - we expect shoppers will absorb them," said Frieder Rotzall, managing director of the German coffee association DKV .
Coffee prices began to move up last month after Brazilian officials suggested the 1997/98 crop may be only 18-20 million bags from around 26 million in 1996/97.
Traders' views were substantially higher, but supplies from Brazil, the largest producer, soon slipped as growers shut their gates, waiting for higher prices to materialise.
This was enough to panic roasters who had reduced stocks to minimum levels in recent years in line with just-in-time buying strategies.
"The fact is that physically the market is relatively tight," said one trader, adding that evidence on the size of the Brazilian crop would set the market direction in the coming months.

Another potential dampener on supplies was a decision by major producers in the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) to expand their export retention programme by a further 1.3 million bags in the first six months of 1997 to push prices higher.
ACPC officials dismissed comments that their policy to hold coffee off the market has backfired, and said there were no immediate plans to review the cuts.

London traders reckon Robusta will benefit from a possible shift in demand from Arabica if roasters change their blend to include more Robusta now that premium on the Arabica has ballooned to 85 cents from 40 in December.
"I think they will have to look at it. The arbitrage is incredible," said one. But others said the scope for such shifts were limited.

"In some cases they might be able to alter the blend slightly in favour of Robustas but the high quality roasts are always Arabica so the roaster really hasn't got much choice. His consumer requires a certain consistency of quality.

"Even in solubles, the housewife likes the jar...to taste pretty much the same as the last jar she bought," he said. "If roasters start mucking around too much it could do severe damage to their sales."
Several European roasters announced plans to raise retail coffee prices this month, saying they were unable to bear higher raw material costs.
In the United States, Procter and Gamble's Folgers Coffee Co said it was raising the price of 13-ounce can of coffee by 15 cents to $2.41 from March.
But British roasters Nestle UK and Whittard of Chelsea, their costs cushioned by the strength of sterling against the dollar, reiterated that they had no plans to lift their prices.
"Any price change disrupts consumption and we are trying to avoid that, even if that means taking some of the pain oursevles," said one roaster representative.
UK roasters mainly produce soluble coffee, which has a higher content of Robusta than ground coffee.
